title: Bananas (per lb)

drivers.name: Price increase to $0.67
drivers.evidence: One prior week at $0.67 (Easter) sold 37% above baseline, but driven by holiday. No non-event week at $0.67 shows uplift. Price increase likely suppresses demand; noise-adjusted estimate shrunk to -10% due to limited evidence.

adjustment.analysis: The baseline (407) is stable, with recent sales near trend. The price is up 3.1% to $0.67, a level not previously seen in the history. The only past week at $0.67 was Easter (2026-03-30), which sold 559 units (vs baseline 407), a 37% uplift. This suggests a price increase may have suppressed demand, but the Easter effect was driven by the holiday, not price. The current week has no event, so the price hike likely reduces demand. The noise-adjusted effect of a price increase at this level is uncertain, but evidence from the one prior $0.67 week (Easter) shows no uplift. The baseline already reflects seasonal trends, so no upward adjustment is justified. A small downside adjustment is warranted.

In the evidence below, 'vs baseline' = actual units / what this same baseline predicted for that week.
It is the multiplier that would have been right, so it maps directly onto median_multiplier.
This product's ordinary weeks already swing about +/-32% around the baseline, so a past effect smaller than that, seen only a few times, is mostly noise. The
'noise-adjusted estimate' is the effect shrunk toward x1.0 for that noise and the number of sightings.
